To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the phase transition for the satisfiability problem is much more complex than previously believed.

(a) the constant probability model is a better model of real world problems than random k-SAT; (b) there is a “constraint gap” in the variable regions of the phase transitions of random k-SAT and related models; (c) the variable regions contain problems orders of magnitude more difficult than the median difficulty; (d) these extraordinarily hard problems can easily dominate mean problem difficulty; (e) these problems will be of use in analyzing the performance of satisfiablity algorithms

there are regions of the phase transition that are orders of magnitude harder to solve, that these regions are due to a constraint gap, that this behaviour is not due to a single variable region, and that these hard problems are not due to an unusually large number of prime implicants.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the analysis of the behaviour of satisfiability algorithms on the hardest problems in a given problem class.
understanding the behaviour of satisfiability algorithms and with the development of new algorithms for satisfiability.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
satisfiability problems are not hard in the middle of a phase transition but rather in the variable regions on the two sides.
the random k-Sat problem is not the hardest random satisfiability problem.
satisfiability problems are not only hard, but also highly variable in difficulty.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the hardest problems in the phase transition region are those with a constraint gap.
we have shown that the random k-Sat model is not a complete description of the behaviour of satisfiability problems.
the hardest problems are not at the phase transition.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the conventional picture of a single phase transition in the SAT problem is wrong and that the SAT problem is actually a collection of different problem classes, with each class exhibiting its own distinct phase transition.

there is a very hard region in the phase transition for all of the problem classes that we investigated and that the conventional wisdom that the phase transition for satisfiability is a simple easy-hard-easy curve is not correct.
the phase transition is not a simple phenomenon.
